messages.author: 91d53d643859f8d6
messages.subject: incorporating posterior distributions from one model into another
parts:
Hi - 

I'm working on a 2-stage model with related outcomes, and the same individuals in each level. 

The outcome of interest for Level 1 is a continuous diagnostic measure meant to indicate whether an individual is infected with a disease. In this level, I'm estimating a bimodal mixture model with an infected and uninfected group. Level 2 is a survival model of the possibly right-censored time at which the individual actually becomes sick with the disease, given demographics and the diagnostic information. The main thing I'm interested in from this level is the posterior probability of infection for each individual, given demographics and her continuous diagnostic measure, to use as an input to the second level. 

I have coded this up, and it works well as a unified model in one stan file, but I'd like to separate the two levels of the model into two separate stan models, so that I can try out alternative specifications for each level. In addition, the current code is hard to maintain, and it would be nice to make it a bit more modular.

I know that one approach would be to just take the posterior mean/median for each individual from stage 1 and use this as a data input stage to the second stage, which I have done successfully before. But this would sacrifice some of the information on variability in the individual diagnoses, which was one of the features I like about the combined model. To be completely hoenst, I'm not sure that this information makes an enormous amount of difference in the eventual outcome, but it seems more correct to me to leave it in than out. 

Any thoughts/suggestions would be greatly appreciated!

Thanks!

-Jon

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] incorporating posterior distributions from one model into another
parts:
This topic of using a posterior from one model as a prior for
another model seems to be trending on stan-users.

There's no easy way to do this directly in Stan. It's not
coherent statistically to just take the samples from the first model
and plug them into the second model because there is typically "feedback"
from the second model to the first. The naive pasting together would
produce the same behavior as cut in BUGS. This is mainly why we haven't
done it and wouldn't recommend it compared to just fitting the joint
model.

(The other area people ask for this is when they trust the first model
more than second model and really do want cut-like behavior, as in
PK/PD models where they know the PK component very well but know the PD
component is misspecified --- they don't want the inferences on the PD
model bleeding back into the PK estimates.)

- Bob

The short answer is that if you think the parameters apply to the old and new data, then it’s best to do full Bayesian inference. If you think the parameters might change, you should put a prior on the “delta” that represents the change.

Hi Folks,

Thanks for all the responses! I think I'm going to stick with the two independent models for the purpose of development and then put them together and do full Bayes on the combined model. Thanks!

One possible mechanical solution I've thought of for exactly this kind of problem would be to write a front-end for R that could use templating (i.e. using brew or something along those lines) to chain together two stan models, taking care to decorate any duplicated variable names, etc. The ideal implementation would look like starting up two rstan runs with their respective input data, i.e. one for each stage, but sampling from the correct posterior by doing all the gnarly C++-style name-mangling in both the R and stan code under the hood. But of course that seems like a lot of work...

Also, this might not be quite the right thread for this, but all of this talk of combined models brings up the question for me of whether to model group-level parameters (in this case a hierarchical model w/about 80 groups) for each level within the same covariance matrix or whether each level should have a separate one. My intuition is that it's ok to put them all together, but wasn't completely sure.

-Jon

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] incorporating posterior distributions from one model into another
parts:
> On May 5, 2015, at 3:40 PM, Krzysztof Sakrejda <krzysztof...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> On Tuesday, May 5, 2015 at 2:51:20 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> This topic of using a posterior from one model as a prior for
> another model seems to be trending on stan-users.
>
> There's no easy way to do this directly in Stan. It's not
> coherent statistically to just take the samples from the first model
> and plug them into the second model because there is typically "feedback"
> from the second model to the first.
>
> I understand the feedback argument, but isn't this also arguing that priors are also not coherent
> statistically? Right now in Stan I can run one analysis, get a posterior for some parameter "theta",
> pick an parametric distribution that approximates the histogram of the samples and use that
> as a prior for my next analysis. This is supposed to be one of the key advantages of Bayes---carrying
> over information from one experiment to another.

Absolutely. And it works out analytically with the case of a stream of
data and conjugate priors. The key is that conjugate priors can be viewed
as data.

In other situations, you're only left with the draws from the posterior
of stage 1, which aren't enough to properly formulate a prior for
stage 2. As you say, you can approximate the prior with a parametric
family, but we don't have any direct mechanism of feeding in the draws
from a previous run to act as a prior to the next run.

It's also problematic when the variables aren't neat sequential priors.

> I think this applies both to multi-stage analyses and to PK/PD style models. It is more limited than a
> joint model but also easier to do model-checking as weird knock-on effects don't get to operate.

What are "knock-on effects"?

The situation in PK/PD is one where you have a PK model

p(theta_PK, y_PK, x_PK)

and a PD model conditioned on the PK parameters

p(theta_PD, y_PD, x_PD | theta_PK)

What the PK/PD modelers want to do is fix the posterior for theta_PK
based only on PK data and priors alpha. If you were to model
everything jointly,

p(theta_PK, theta_PD, y_PK, y_PD, x_PK, x_PD)

the PD data and model model would affect the estimates for theta_PK.
That is, the theta_PK isn't a prior for theta_PD with y_PD and x_PD just
being more of the same kind of PK data.

At least I think that's what's going on!

- Bob

I posted my original response because I think the situation where you can approximate the posterior draws with a normal
distribution is pretty common.  If you want to hedge your bets about whether the prior is reasonable you can even weaken
your posterior by using a t-distribution with moderate degrees of freedom or inflate the variance you originally estimated. 
For more complex posteriors a mixture of normals, or a mixture of gammas could work as well.  In any case, there's a
common problem and a workable solution and I'm not sure why it doesn't get recommended more often.

It's also problematic when the variables aren't neat sequential priors.

> I think this applies both to multi-stage analyses and to PK/PD style models.  It is more limited than a
> joint model but also easier to do model-checking as weird knock-on effects don't get to operate.

What are "knock-on effects"?  


 

The situation in PK/PD is one where you have a PK model

  p(theta_PK, y_PK, x_PK)

and a PD model conditioned on the PK parameters

  p(theta_PD, y_PD, x_PD | theta_PK)

What the PK/PD modelers want to do is fix the posterior for theta_PK
based only on PK data and priors alpha.  If you were to model
everything jointly,

  p(theta_PK, theta_PD, y_PK, y_PD, x_PK, x_PD)

the PD data and model model would affect the estimates for theta_PK.

That's what I called a knock-on effect, I claim ESL as my excuse for weird english.  In this case
I would say the following is fine:

1) use p(theta_PK, y_PK, x_PK) to generate a posterior sample of theta_PK
2) approximate that posterior with a parametric family
3) use the approximate posterior distribution as a fixed prior for the PD model.

That is, the theta_PK isn't a prior for theta_PD with y_PD and x_PD just
being more of the same kind of PK data.

I don't think this scenario is any different from any other two-stage analysis, why
would the implications be different just because the second stage is for a different analysis?

Krzysztof

At least I think that's what's going on!

- Bob

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] incorporating posterior distributions from one model into another
parts:
I posted my original response because I think the situation where you can approximate the posterior draws with a normal
distribution is pretty common.  If you want to hedge your bets about whether the prior is reasonable you can even weaken
your posterior by using a t-distribution with moderate degrees of freedom or inflate the variance you originally estimated.  
For more complex posteriors a mixture of normals, or a mixture of gammas could work as well.  In any case, there's a 
common problem and a workable solution and I'm not sure why it doesn't get recommended more often.

Because these simple parametric forms are _terrible_ at capturing the nonlinear
correlations common to realistic posterior distributions.  Besides if these functional
forms were so good we’d just be fitting them to the data (a la variational bays or
expectation propagation) and then doing all of our expectations analytically.
There’s a reason why a huge chunk of the statistical community is studying 
Sequential Monte Carlo and not just fitting functional forms.

In this PK/PD setting, they explicitly *don't* want it to be a typical
two-stage analysis. In the typical two stager you get:

Stage 1: prior(1) -> data(1) -> posterior(1)

Stage 2: posterior(1) -> data(2) -> posterior(2)

and now posterior(2) won't match posterior(1). But what you want with
cut is to *fix* posterior(1) and not let data(2) update it.

Instead, that posterior(1) isn't a prior for data(2), but another joint
parameter, and they don't want data(2) messing with, it so they can't just
make posterior(1) a parameter in the Stage 2 program.

- Bob

On Wednesday, May 6, 2015 at 6:04:35 PM UTC-4, Michael Betancourt wrote:

I posted my original response because I think the situation where you can approximate the posterior draws with a normal
distribution is pretty common.  If you want to hedge your bets about whether the prior is reasonable you can even weaken
your posterior by using a t-distribution with moderate degrees of freedom or inflate the variance you originally estimated.  
For more complex posteriors a mixture of normals, or a mixture of gammas could work as well.  In any case, there's a 
common problem and a workable solution and I'm not sure why it doesn't get recommended more often.

Because these simple parametric forms are _terrible_ at capturing the nonlinear
correlations common to realistic posterior distributions.

But we do advocate weak priors even though those are also terrible at capturing correlations.  My point is
that the boundary is as clear as your answer makes it out to be.  If I notice that my
posterior is banana-shaped, I can come up with an informative banana-shaped parametric form
for my posterior. If on the other hand, I miss that sort of multiplicative identifiability problem,
I might specify harmless-seeming weak priors that really impact my analysis.  In either case the
only way you find out is by examining the posterior samples (if you're lucky) or the functional
form of the posterior.

Besides if these functional
forms were so good we’d just be fitting them to the data (a la variational bays or
expectation propagation) and then doing all of our expectations analytically.
There’s a reason why a huge chunk of the statistical community is studying 
Sequential Monte Carlo and not just fitting functional forms.
Fair enough, I can see that it's a preferable approach.

> I don't think this scenario is any different from any other two-stage analysis, why
> would the implications be different just because the second stage is for a different analysis?

In this PK/PD setting, they explicitly *don't* want it to be a typical
two-stage analysis.  In the typical two stager you get:

  Stage 1:  prior(1) -> data(1) -> posterior(1)

  Stage 2: posterior(1) -> data(2) -> posterior(2)

and now posterior(2) won't match posterior(1).  But what you want with
cut is to *fix* posterior(1) and not let data(2) update it.

Instead, that posterior(1) isn't a prior for data(2), but another joint
parameter, and they don't want data(2) messing with, it so they can't just
make posterior(1) a parameter in the Stage 2 program.

B is data(1), D is data(2), A is the parameter of interest from stage 1. 
Then the  PK/PD situation is like this:

p(A) -> p(A|B) approximated by q(A) -> p(C|A,D) or if you re-do the PK experiment, you could also do:
p(A) -> p(A|B) approximated by q(A) -> p(A|D), approximately p(A|B,D)

I think these are parallel situations.  Does cut-like functionality really do anything different?
I guess it lets you use the samples directly rather than the approximation which Michael has already
pointed is an improvement out so maybe that's what I'm missing.

Krzysztof

 

- Bob

I didn't follow that notation or what C was.

But it's just about feedback --- hence the name "cut". It's not about
how good or bad the approximation is --- it's about holding some
distributions fixed (not variables fixed, but distributions). Rather than me
trying again, I'd suggest looking at this:

http://www.math.helsinki.fi/openbugs/IceBUGS/Presentations/BestIceBUGS.pdf

It's the example they use in the BUGS book, too.

- Bob
